---
title: Decision Trees
output: pdf_document
---

Management will adjust their decisions based on new information. Information
about a successful launch of a new product will influence the decision to
expand the product to new markets. Each individual choice the manager has is
called a real option. A project can essentially be viewed as a series of real
options, leading to valuation approaches beyond the basic present value
methodology.

We can return to the Solar Electronics Corporation (SEC) and their
solar-powered engines to demonstrate how decision trees can represent a project
that is based on a series of decisions. Imagine before the launch of the
production of the solar-powered engines, SEC wants to test market the product
to see how the market will respond to the engine. SEC builds some prototype
engines and conducts test marketing. Based on the results of the test
marketing, SEC will decide to carry through with the production of the new
engine.

So the first decision SEC must make is whether or not to conduct the test
marketing. If SEC decides to go ahead with the study, based on the study, SEC
needs to decide whether or not to invest the \$1,500 million to start
production of the solar-powered engine.

We can represent this project, and its series of options, as a decision tree.
In order to construct this decision tree, it is best to work backwards and
consider each branch of the tree.

First let's assume that the test marketing was successful (75% probability). We
already know the NPV for the production project for five years. Assuming an
investment of \$1,500 million, with a cash flow of \$900 million for five years
and a required return rate of 15\%.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{NPV} &= -\$1{,}500 + \sum^{5}_{t=1}{\frac{\$900}{(1.15)^t}}\\
  &= -\$1{,}500 + \$900 \times \text{PVIA}(.15, 5)\\
  &= \$1{,}517
\end{aligned}
$$

If the test marketing is successful, the positive NPV value means that SEC
should go ahead with production.

Next we assume that the test marketing was a failure (25% probability). Again
we calculate the NPV using the investment of \$1,500 million. The book does not
give the cash flow or the calculation but does give the final NPV as -\$3,611
million. Because the NPV is negative SEC should not proceed with production.

Assuming that the test marketing will take a year to conduct and analyze, SEC
needs to decide whether or not to conduct the test marketing one year before
production is to take place. Let's assume that the test marketing will take
\$100 million to conduct. We can find the total expected payoff:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Expected payoff} &= (\text{success} \times \text{payoff})
  + (\text{failure} \times \text{payoff})\\
  &= (.75 \times \$1{,}517) + (.25 \times \$0)\\
  &= \$1{,}138
\end{aligned}
$$

The payoff for the failure branch is zero because we calculated the NPV to be
-\$3,611 and thus we expect not to proceed with full-scale production. The NPV
of testing computed at Date 0 (in millions):

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{NPV} &= -\$100 + \frac{\$1{,}138}{1.15}\\
  &= \$890
\end{aligned}
$$

\$1,517 is the NPV at date 1, when the production decision is made. The
expected payoff (\$1,138) is a date-1 value, and we divide by 1.15 to bring
it to date 0. Because the NPV is positive, SEC should proceed with the test
marketing.

If SEC were to produce regardless of the test result, we would calculate the
expected payoff:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Expected payoff} &= (\text{success} \times \text{payoff})
  + (\text{failure} \times \text{payoff})\\
  &= (.75 \times \$1{,}517) + (.25 \times -\$3{,}611)\\
  &= \$235
\end{aligned}
$$

The NPV of testing would be:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{NPV} &= -\$100 + \frac{\$235}{1.15}\\
  &= \$104
\end{aligned}
$$

The value of walking away from the project is \$890 - \$104 = \$786 million.
This is the option to abandon if the test fails.

The same discount rate was used for both the test marketing and the investment
decision for production. You may want to use a higher discount rate for the
test marketing decision because it is likely to be riskier than the investment
decision.

# Conclusion

In this specific example SEC needed to make the following two decisions:

1. Whether to develop and test the solar-powered jet engine.
2. Whether to invest for full-scale production following the results of the test.

In this situation, a decision tree is a natural approach for analysis. Financial
options are valued with a similar tree structure (the binomial model). The
difference is the discounting: instead of a risk-adjusted rate like SEC's 15%,
option pricing values the option relative to the underlying stock and discounts
at the risk-free rate.
